bio.en: Annie Duke is the author of the bestsellers Thinking in Bets and Quit: The Power of Knowing When to Walk Away, a former professional poker player who won over $4 million, and a special partner at First Round Capital.
bio.zh: Annie Duke 是畅销书《赌注思维》（Thinking in Bets）和《退出：懂得何时放手的力量》（Quit）的作者，曾经的职业扑克玩家（赢得超 400 万美元），也是 First Round Capital 的特别合伙人。

summary.en: Annie explains the importance of making intuition explicit so you can discover when it's wrong, and reframes meetings around discovery, discussion, and decision rather than just talking. She introduces pre-mortems paired with kill criteria and argues there is no such thing as a long feedback loop if you identify correlated signals. The conversation draws on lessons from her friend Daniel Kahneman about improving decision quality in companies.
summary.zh: Annie 解释了把直觉“显性化”的重要性，这样你才能发现它何时出错，并把会议重新定义为发现、讨论和决策，而非只是空谈。她介绍了配合“终止标准”的事前复盘（pre-mortem），并认为只要你找到相关信号，就不存在“长反馈循环”。对话借用了她已故好友、心理学家 Daniel Kahneman 的洞见，探讨如何提升企业的决策质量。

turns.speaker: Annie Duke
turns.en: It's so incredibly necessary in improving decision quality to take what's implicit and make it explicit. It's not that intuition is crap, your intuition is sometimes right. If you don't make it explicit, then you don't get to find out when it's wrong.
turns.zh: 为了提高决策质量，将隐含的内容变得明确是非常必要的。并不是说直觉是垃圾，你的直觉有时是对的。如果你不明确地表达出来，那么你就无法发现它何时是错误的。

turns.speaker: Annie Duke
turns.en: People generally think the purpose of a meeting is for three things, discover, discuss, decide. The only thing that's ever supposed to happen in a meeting is the discussion part.
turns.zh: 人们普遍认为会议的目的是为了三件事：发现、讨论、决定。会议中唯一应该发生的事情就是讨论部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that comes up in product a lot is this idea of pre-mortems.
turns.zh: 产品中经常出现的就是事前剖析的想法。

turns.speaker: Annie Duke
turns.en: So a pre-mortem, it's great only if you set up kill criteria. Commit to actions that you're going to take if you see those signals.
turns.zh: 因此，事前剖析，只有设置杀戮标准才有意义。承诺在看到这些信号时将采取的行动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have a very interesting framework for how to think about decision quality when the outcome is very long-term.
turns.zh: 当结果非常长期时，您有一个非常有趣的框架来思考如何考虑决策质量。

turns.speaker: Annie Duke
turns.en: There is no such thing as a long feedback loop. And the way you choose to shorten the feedback loop is to say, what are the things that are correlated with the outcome that I eventually desire?
turns.zh: 不存在长反馈循环这样的事情。你选择缩短反馈循环的方式是说，哪些事情与我最终想要的结果相关？

(00:38:02): And you could do it in some way, like how many sprints do you think is going to take whatever language you want to use? turns.zh: 是的。所以我认为一般来说，当你创建最初的决策标题时，人们确实在讨论一些他们认为对做出决定特别重要的事情。我们发现的一件事是，有时他们的直觉是绝对正确的。他们所讨论的事情具有令人难以置信的预测性，不仅对他们而言，对其他合作伙伴也是如此。但有时它根本无法预测，而且这些都是同样令人震惊的情况。假设你正在讨论某件事，有时你在讨论的事情对你和所有其他合作伙伴来说是有预测性的，它实际上可以很好地预测公司的表现。但有时，当你真的就某件事争论不休时，这不仅对其他合作伙伴没有预测作用，对你也没有预测作用。 (01:03:33)：我认为理解这一点真正重要的是，我们的直觉有时是正确的，有时是错误的，这就是为什么在提高决策质量方面非常有必要将隐含的内容变得明确。这并不是说直觉是垃圾，你的直觉是完全错误的，我的意思是显然，这不可能是真的。我们会死，对吧？所以你的直觉有时是对的，但有时也是错的。如果你不明确地表达出来，那么你就无法发现它何时是错误的。 (01:04:07)：你无法发现它何时偏离基地，那是一场灾难。因此，我认为真正有趣的是，您对这个特定因素非常重要有同样的热情和信心。有时是，有时不是。这太令人惊讶了，因为我们谈论的是真正的专家，他们是伟大的，而且我认为我们都有关于直觉的直觉，对吧？你只是凭直觉知道，如果他们如此出色，那么显然他们对重要事物的直觉一定很好，但不一定。事情就是这样，不一定。是的，我认为这可能是最令人兴奋的事情。

turns.en: I wanted to touch on a different framework that I've heard a lot of companies actually using, and something that comes up in product a lot is this idea of pre-mortems, which is essentially think ahead of time what might go wrong. Can you talk about this? Because I think that it's something that's easy to implement, really powerful, and a lot of people are actually doing this.
turns.zh: 我想谈谈一个不同的框架，我听说很多公司实际使用过这个框架，产品中经常出现的就是事前剖析的想法，这本质上是提前考虑可能会出现问题的地方。你能谈谈这个吗？因为我认为它很容易实现，非常强大，而且很多人实际上正在这样做。

turns.speaker: Annie Duke
turns.en: Yes, okay. So a pre-mortem is great, but only if you attach a pre-commitment with it. So I just want to be super clear about that. What you find with pre-mortems, this actually work. I actually did this work with Maurice Schweitzer and Linnea Gandhi, who are both at Penn. Then when you have people do pre-mortems, it generally doesn't actually change their plan very much or it changed their behavior. So I think that we have the feeling that if you do a pre-mortem and you think what are the ways that things might go wrong, that that's going to change your plan, but probably not unless you're specifically using it for that purpose and you say, "Okay, we're going to do this, but let's think about how we might change our plan in light of this information." But I think what's actually more important than that is what a pre-mortem allows you to do is to set up kill criteria. (01:06:18): So kill criteria are just a set of signals that you might see that would tell you that it's time to pivot or stop because once we actually launch something, we're very, very slow to decide to quit. I'm sure that everybody has felt that way before. Things go on way too long, even like they're over budget and you've blown the timeline. And when you finally shut it down, you realize you should have done it a lot earlier. And this is true across the board because of a variety of biases. The most well-known, and probably the biggest influence is something called sunk cost, which is that feeling, but then I'll have wasted all the time and effort that I've put into this already. So it's taking into account what you've put in in the past and deciding whether to continue on in the future. So what we want to do is actually just get better at that thing. So understanding that when you've gotten to the pre-mortem process, you probably are going to launch it, like it's probably going to be the case. (01:07:22): Use the pre-mortem to set up kill criteria. So I'll give you an example from a sales team that I worked with. Basically, I sent them out a prompt, all the IC is a prompt that was, imagine that you got a lead through an RFP or RFI and you worked on it for six months. And now, it's six months later and the deal is dead. Looking back, you realized they were early signals that that was going to be the case, what were they. So this is a pre-mortem. What are the things that you saw that would tell you that this was going to go south? And they came up with all sorts of ideas. Notice this doesn't mean they're not going to start off pursuing the lead, right? But they saw, they came up with all sorts of signals. So I'll just give you three of them. (01:08:12): The RFP RFI was clearly written with a competitor in mind, so they felt that was a very bad signal that was probably going to go badly. Another one was the customer didn't want to demo, they only wanted to talk about price. Obviously, that's quite bad. And another one was after the first few meetings, they couldn't get a decision maker in the room, right? So it was a much longer list than this, but those are three. So for each of those, that now becomes a kill criteria if I see this thing and now you attach an action with it. So in the case of price, they actually just said, "We should kill it." If they literally don't want to demo and they're only asking about price, they're just trying to beat up somebody else on price like we're a box-checking exercise. So there, they just said, "We're going to kill it. We're not going to pursue the deal anymore." (01:08:59): So this is great because salespeople will pursue deals forever and leadership is like, "Well, why did you stop pursuing that deal?" And they get in trouble for it. So this is going to help with that problem, right? In the case of the RFP RFI was written with a competitor in mind, they have an action associated with that as well, which is ask them directly if they're working with a competitor and how far down the road they are, depending on the answer you would kill or pursue. In the case of we couldn't get a decision maker in the room, offer up executive alignment at the next meeting. And if they say sure, great. And if they say no, kill. (01:09:35): So that's actually what I feel is the best use of a pre-mortem is to say, I'm going to try to figure out what those signals are along the way that things are going badly. And now instead of just hoping that when I see those signals, I actually act rationally, which is a hope that it will not come true. That's why there's many people who climb Everest in the middle of a blizzard, even though they shouldn't be doing that. Use the pre-mortem to now create structure around those signals that you've spotted and commit to actions that you're going to take if you see those signals. And I think that's the best use of a pre-mortem.
turns.zh: 是的，好的。因此，事前剖析是很好的选择，但前提是您必须附上预先承诺。所以我只想说得非常清楚。你在事前剖析中发现，这实际上是有效的。实际上，我与宾夕法尼亚大学的莫里斯·史怀哲和林尼·甘地一起完成了这项工作。然后，当你让人们进行事前剖析时，通常实际上不会改变他们的计划或改变他们的行为。因此，我认为我们有一种感觉，如果你进行事前剖析，并且你认为事情可能会出错的方式是什么，那么这将改变你的计划，但可能不会，除非你专门将其用于该目的，并且你说：“好吧，我们将这样做，但让我们考虑如何根据这些信息改变我们的计划。”但我认为实际上比这更重要的是事前剖析允许你设置杀死标准。 (01:06:18)：因此，终止标准只是您可能会看到的一组信号，这些信号会告诉您是时候进行调整或停止了，因为一旦我们真正启动某些内容，我们就会非常非常缓慢地决定退出。我相信每个人都曾有过这样的感受。事情持续的时间太长，甚至超出了预算，而且你已经超出了时间表。当你最终关闭它时，你意识到你应该早点做。由于存在各种偏见，这在所有方面都是如此。最著名的，也可能是最大的影响是所谓的沉没成本，就是这种感觉，但那样我就浪费了我已经投入于此的所有时间和精力。因此，它会考虑您过去的投入并决定未来是否继续。所以我们想做的实际上就是在这件事上做得更好。因此，要明白，当您进入事前剖析过程时，您可能会启动它，就像情况可能会如此一样。 (01:07:22)：使用事前剖析来设置杀戮标准。因此，我将举一个我曾合作过的销售团队的例子。基本上，我向他们发出了一个提示，所有 IC 都是一个提示，想象一下，您通过 RFP 或 RFI 获得了线索，并且您为此工作了六个月。现在，六个月过去了，这笔交易已经结束了。回想起来，你意识到它们是事情将会发生的早期信号，它们是什么。所以这是一个预验。你所看到的哪些事情会告诉你事情将会向南发展？他们想出了各种各样的想法。请注意，这并不意味着他们不会开始追赶领先地位，对吧？但他们看到了，他们提出了各种各样的信号。所以我只给你其中三个。 (01:08:12)：RFP RFI 显然是在考虑竞争对手的情况下编写的，因此他们认为这是一个非常糟糕的信号，可能会变得很糟糕。另一种是客户不想演示，只想谈价格。显然，这很糟糕。另一个问题是在最初的几次会议之后，他们无法在房间里找到决策者，对吧？所以这个列表比这个长得多，但只有三个。因此，对于其中的每一个，如果我看到这个东西并且现在你附加一个动作，那么现在就成为杀死标准。因此，在价格方面，他们实际上只是说，“我们应该取消它。”如果他们真的不想演示，而只是询问价格，那么他们只是想在价格上击败其他人，就像我们在进行检查练习一样。因此，他们只是说，“我们要终止它。我们不会再继续推进这项交易了。” (01:08:59)：所以这很棒，因为销售人员将永远追求交易，而领导层会说，“那么，你为什么停止追求这笔交易？”他们因此而陷入麻烦。所以这将有助于解决这个问题，对吧？如果 RFP RFI 是在考虑竞争对手的情况下编写的，那么他们也有与之相关的行动，即直接询问他们是否正在与竞争对手合作以及他们的进展有多远，具体取决于您想要杀死或追求的答案。如果我们无法在房间里找到决策者，请在下次会议上提出高管协调。如果他们说当然，那就太好了。如果他们拒绝，那就杀掉。 (01:09:35)：所以这实际上是我认为事前剖析的最佳用途，就是说，我将尝试找出在事情进展糟糕的过程中这些信号是什么。现在，我不再只是希望当我看到这些信号时，我实际上会理性地行动，这是希望它不会实现。这就是为什么有很多人在暴风雪中攀登珠穆朗玛峰，尽管他们不应该这样做。现在，使用事前分析来围绕您发现的信号创建结构，并承诺在看到这些信号时将采取的行动。我认为这是事前剖析的最佳用途。

turns.speaker: Annie Duke
turns.en: So the data is pretty strong that by the time you quit, it's probably long after the [inaudible 01:11:37]. And it's really just because, look, when we start things, we're starting things under difficult circumstances, which come from the uncertainty of the decision to start something. So when we start something, luck is going to have an influence on the outcome, which obviously, we have no control over because luck isn't in our control. And then there's also hidden information. So what happens is that after the fact, we know that we're going to learn new information and it can make it very hard to start things because we want to be more sure than we actually need to be. It's why Bezos has the 70% role to try to roll people back and be willing to accept that uncertainty in the starting decision. Now the good news is that when you learn that new stuff and the new stuff that you learn is, "Ooh, if I had known this, I wouldn't have started it", you have the option to quit generally. (01:12:28): So that's the good news. The bad news is that the same difficulties that apply to the decision to start apply to the decision to stop. In other words, we're making that decision under uncertainty as well. So we're not going to know for sure whether it would've turned out well or poorly unless we continue to do the thing that we already started. And we don't like to walk away from things unless we know for sure. So as Richard Thaler put it, most people won't quit until it actually isn't a decision. In other words, the whole thing is blown up, the startup has no money, or you're up on Everest and the blizzard is literally upon you and you're stuck in it. Or I think as he said, until you've fallen in the crevasse already, then you'll make the decision to quit because then you know how it was really bad. So people generally, for example, don't quit their jobs until they feel they have no other choice or relationships or projects or products that they're developing, it all applies because we want to know for sure. (01:13:35): And then on top of that is the fact that there is this issue of sunk cost, which is when we walk away, we feel like we'll have wasted everything that we've already put into what we're doing. But of course, waste is a prospective problem, not a retrospective one, even if we treat it like a retrospective one because it's the prospective one. Well, if you wouldn't start this today, then that means that everything that you're putting into this going forward is the actual waste, right? But we do that all the time. We go forward with things that we ought not to be going forward with because we're trying to protect the resources that we've already sunk into it in the past. Then there's other issues that have to do with, for example, endowment, the ownership over the things that we've built. This is particularly bad in product because we're building things. (01:14:18): And once we build things, we own them. And once we own them, we don't want to give them up and we actually value them more highly than identical things that we don't own. And then there's issues of internal and external validity, which is really just a fancy way to say your identity. How do other people view you? How do you view yourself? Do you feel like you failed? And what that means is that by the time, there's so many biases against stopping that by the time you're actually even thinking about quitting, it's probably already past the time that you ought to have quit. But we'll still continue on until we know for sure we didn't have any choice because here's the thing. When you walk away from something and someone's like, "Hey, why'd you stop that?" And you're like, "Oh, I had no choice" and you tell them everything that went wrong and, nobody's going to question you. (01:15:04): They're going to be like, "Oh, well, it sounds like you put in your best effort." But if you walk away early, people are like, "What?" So just quickly, I'll tell you I think just one of the best stories of this that I've got in my pocket here. Let me pull it out before the end. So Stewart Butterfield creating a product called Glitch, and Glitch is a massive multiplayer online world-building cooperative game. Releases it, this is in the aughts, and it's like a huge hit with the critics. It's Monty Python meets Dr. Seuss, it's an incredible whatever. They're getting tons and tons of great word of mouth and PR not doing any paid marketing. They have incredible investors in Andreessen Horowitz and Accel, they have $6 million in the bank and they 5,000 have diehard users, meaning users who use the game who play over 20 hours a week. (01:16:04): The issue is that customer acquisition was a beast that for every one person who was playing over 20 hours a week, there were between 95 and 99 people who came for five minutes and left. So obviously, this is a customer acquisition problem, which everybody knows. So they make an agreement in 2012 that they're going to do paid marketing, which they do for six weeks. And during that six weeks, their acquisition of new users, it's growing like six to 7% week over week, which is amazing. And at the end of that six weeks, this is November of 2012, at the end of that six weeks, that Monday morning, Stewart Butterfield writes a note to his investors and co-founders and says, "I woke up this morning with the dead certainty that Glitch was over." (01:16:58): Now notice nobody would do this in this case, right? But this is what happened is that the issue is that you really have to see is this worthwhile or not? Would I start this today? That's a forecast of the future, right? And what he did was some back-of-the-envelope math, and he said, "Look, if we continue to acquire customers at the weight that we've been acquiring them at the cost that we've been acquiring them, it's going to be 31 weeks until we break even." But that's an absurd assumption because customer acquisition costs, it's going to go up. Cap has to rise because we're going to saturate the core gaming market, so it's got to rise. So what he realized at that point was that this was not a venture scale business, and he was in this for a venture scale business. So even though nobody else saw that he was supposed to shut it down, he saw he was supposed to shut it down. (01:17:45): And not only that, he saw that he was supposed to shut it down for his employees who were working for equity, and he had now realized that the equity wasn't worth their time and that it wasn't fair to them to keep going with it. So he shuts it down. Obviously, that feels... Who does that? Right? And he will actually tell you that he knows he should have shut it down before the marketing push, but he needed the marketing push to prove it to himself that he was seeing the future clearly. Now, the code to this story just quickly is two days later, he's like, "Well, I'm a startup guy. I want to start something", and he's got this internal communication tool that his team is using in order to develop this product that everybody loves. And he says, "Actually, they really like that. Maybe that should be the next product." (01:18:29): So he goes and talks to the investors, they roll their money over into that. And that thing, which had no name at the time, now gets a name which is searchable log of all company knowledge, which is Slack. And so I think this is the important thing to realize is that we get so focused on, "But what about everything that I've put into it?" When what we forget is that when you're doing something, there's not just the cost of doing something that's not worthwhile that's direct, but there's also the cost of not being able to devote your attention to other opportunities that might be available to you. And as smart as Stewart Butterfield is, he couldn't see Slack until he quit Glitch. And that is a true cost that he would've born of continuing with Glitch. If he had continued with Glitch, Slack would not be something that we're all using today.

01:11:37]。这实际上只是因为，看，当我们开始做某事时，我们是在困难的情况下开始做事的，这来自于开始做某事的决定的不确定性。因此，当我们开始做某事时，运气就会对结果产生影响，显然，我们无法控制这一点，因为运气不在我们的控制范围内。然后还有隐藏信息。因此，事后发生的情况是，我们知道我们将学习新信息，这会使开始工作变得非常困难，因为我们想要比实际需要的更加确定。这就是为什么贝索斯有 70% 的角色试图让人们倒退并愿意接受开始决策中的不确定性。现在的好消息是，当你学到新东西时，你学到的新东西是，“哦，如果我早知道这个，我就不会开始了”，你通常可以选择退出。 (01:12:28)：这就是好消息。坏消息是，做出开始的决定时遇到的困难同样适用于停止的决定。换句话说，我们也是在不确定的情况下做出这个决定的。因此，除非我们继续做我们已经开始的事情，否则我们无法确定结果是好是坏。除非我们确实知道，否则我们不喜欢放弃事情。因此，正如理查德·塞勒所说，大多数人不会放弃，直到它实际上不是一个决定。换句话说，整个事情都被炸毁了，初创公司没有钱，或者你在珠穆朗玛峰上，暴风雪确实向你袭来，你被困在其中。或者我认为正如他所说，直到你已经陷入裂缝，然后你才会做出退出的决定，因为那时你就知道事情有多糟糕。因此，例如，人们通常不会辞去工作，直到他们感到没有其他选择或他们正在开发的关系、项目或产品，这一切都适用，因为我们想确定。 (01:13:35)：最重要的是，存在沉没成本的问题，即当我们离开时，我们感觉我们已经浪费了我们已经投入到正在做的事情中的一切。但当然，浪费是一个前瞻性问题，而不是一个回顾性问题，即使我们把它当作一个回顾性问题来对待，因为它是一个前瞻性问题。好吧，如果你今天不开始，那就意味着你今后投入的一切都是真正的浪费，对吧？但我们一直这样做。我们继续做那些我们不应该做的事情，因为我们试图保护我们过去已经投入的资源。还有其他与我们所建造的东西的所有权有关的问题。这在产品中尤其糟糕，因为我们正在构建东西。 (01:14:18)：一旦我们建造了东西，我们就拥有它们。一旦我们拥有它们，我们就不想放弃它们，而且我们实际上比我们不拥有的相同东西更看重它们。然后还有内部和外部有效性的问题，这实际上只是表达你的身份的一种奇特方式。其他人如何看待你？你如何看待自己？你觉得自己失败了吗？这意味着，到了那时，有太多反对戒烟的偏见，以至于当你真正考虑戒烟时，可能已经过了你应该戒烟的时间了。但我们仍然会继续下去，直到我们确定我们别无选择，因为事情就是这样。当你离开某件事时，有人会问：“嘿，你为什么要阻止它？”你会说，“哦，我别无选择”，然后你告诉他们所有出错的事情，没有人会质疑你。 Python) 遇见苏斯博士 (Dr. Seuss)，这真是令人难以置信。他们在不进行任何付费营销的情况下获得了大量的口碑和公关。他们拥有 Andreessen Horowitz 和 Accel 等令人难以置信的投资者，他们在银行有 600 万美元的存款，还有 5,000 名顽固用户，这意味着每周玩游戏超过 20 小时的用户。 (01:16:04)：问题是，客户获取是一场猛兽，每一个每周玩 20 给他的投资者和联合创始人写了一张便条，说道：“今天早上我醒来时，我确信 Glitch 已经结束了。” (01:16:58)：现在请注意，在这种情况下没有人会这样做，对吗？但这就是发生的事情，问题是你真的必须看看这是否值得？我今天就开始这个吗？这是对未来的预测，对吗？他所做的是一些粗略的计算，他说，“看，如果我们继续以我们一直以来以成本获取客户的重量来获取客户，那么我们需要 31
